interface_detail: The three cited pages price the product and state the KYC gate; none of them records the wire protocol or a public API, so this record does not assert socks5 or http-proxy. The token list is left at unknown rather than guessed.
tooling: The cited pages describe no SDK, CLI or rclone-style backend, and no wrapper is needed to judge the provider: what stands in the way is the identity gate, not tooling. Whether a given client can dial the issued endpoint is unestablished here, because the protocol is not recorded.
chaining: An egress hop in front of the Workers AI gateway: about 45 GB a month across about 599,000 requests leaves through a proxy endpoint, so the per-proxy plan's 50 GB fair-use ceiling per proxy sits 5 GB above the whole workload, and the per-GB plan would bill about USD 90 a month at USD 2.00/GB.

limits.value: 50 GB fair-use threshold per proxy per month on the USD 59/proxy/month unlimited-bandwidth plan
USD 2.00 per GB flat, prepaid in blocks of 25 GB (USD 50), 50 GB (USD 100), 100 GB (USD 200) and 200 GB (USD 400): bytes past a block are another purchase

limits_note: The national-id KYC gate is a real constraint but is not one of the seven limit kinds; it lives in identity_cost and is the reason for the verdict. No request-rate, per-IP-shaping or pull-count limit appears on the three pages read.
binding_note: At 45 GB a month the byte meter is the only constraint the pages state, and it fails first: one proxy's 50 GB fair-use ceiling covers the workload with 5 GB of headroom, so a month that runs hot needs a second proxy, and the per-GB plan turns the same 45 GB into about USD 90 a month. No request-rate or per-IP limit is published, so none can fail before it.

identity_cost.detail: KYC is mandatory before first use: You must complete identity verification (Tier 1) before you can use the proxies. The check is a document check against a national id, so the account is bound to one named person. The tier label implies further levels above Tier 1; those were not read. No second gate such as a card is recorded on the cited pages.

reliability_note: Their marketing graphic shows the exit 100.64.12.7 AS21928, but 100.64.12.7 is RFC 6598 carrier-shared space and RIPE returns no ASN for it, so that address is an illustration rather than a dialable exit; their other displayed exit, 172.58.14.102, does resolve to AS21928 T-Mobile USA, so the carrier claim holds where the sample address does not.
confidence_note: Every field the verdict rests on is read from the vendor's own pages on 2026-10-24: the price, the 50 GB fair-use threshold and the Tier 1 KYC sentence. The only measurement here is the two-address RIPE lookup, which settles the graphic and not the verdict. Measured would need an approved Tier 1 account, a session through an issued endpoint and a byte count.

evidence.proved: Per GB USD 2.00 flat with block prices USD 50/25 GB, USD 100/50 GB, USD 200/100 GB and USD 400/200 GB; per proxy USD 59/proxy/month with unlimited bandwidth and a 50 GB fair-use threshold per proxy per month.
Identity verification is a required step of getting an account, which makes this a national-id class registration rather than an email or phone signup.

The per-proxy plan's unlimited bandwidth is qualified by a 50 GB fair-use threshold per proxy per month, and the page carries the sentence You must complete identity verification (Tier 1) before you can use the proxies.
RIPE Stat returns announced:false and an empty asns[] for 100.64.12.7 and places it in 100.64.0.0/10 Shared Address Space (according to [RFC 6598]), so the address in the graphic cannot be an exit.
RIPE Stat aligns 172.58.14.102 to the less-specific 172.58.8.0/21 and returns asn 21928, holder T-MOBILE-AS21928 - T-Mobile USA, so the carrier behind the other displayed exit is real.

price_per_tb_month: not quoted per TB: USD 2.00 per GB flat metered, or USD 59 per proxy per month with a 50 GB fair-use threshold
notes: Two pricing shapes are kept in one record because they are the same product and the difference is the point: the per-proxy plan's unlimited bandwidth is bounded by a 50 GB fair-use threshold, which is the number that matters at 45 GB a month, and splitting the record would hide that. Candidates for why the product fails, tested in order: (1) the identity gate, confirmed by the help page sentence on Tier 1 verification before first use; (2) the volume ceiling, real but not disqualifying at 45 GB, since one proxy covers the workload with 5 GB of headroom; (3) the exits being synthetic, refuted for 172.58.14.102, which RIPE aligns to AS21928 T-Mobile USA, and confirmed only for the graphic's 100.64.12.7, which sits in RFC 6598 shared space with no ASN. The address finding rests on one lookup per address on 2026-10-24, taken from RIPE Stat's prefix-overview rather than from a request through an issued endpoint; a session through an approved account would settle it and nothing else available here would. A third-party comparison blog (caproxy, 2025-12-08) claims a free version covering up to 5 ports; no vendor page read here confirms it, so free_tier records what the vendor prices and nothing more, and a vendor page naming a free plan would move it. The interface token is unknown because none of the cited pages records the protocol, and because scripts/dossier/schema.json's interface enum has no socks5, http-proxy, api or web-ui value for a record to use; validate.py rejects those tokens, so the protocol belongs in interface_detail until the enum is extended.

extras.rung_note: The exit sits in a carrier's mobile address pool (AS21928 T-Mobile USA) and the gate is a national-id KYC rather than a carrier contract, so the distinguishing property is the address registration class, one rung above a bare ASN.
